title: FOLFOXIRI

agents.name: Irinotecan
agents.explanation: The body converts irinotecan into SN-38. This traps an enzyme called topoisomerase I while DNA is being copied, causing damage that can stop cancer cells dividing. Normal bowel and blood-forming cells can also be affected.
agents.watch: Tell the nurse immediately about cramps, sweating or diarrhoea during the infusion. Diarrhoea starting later needs the separate written treatment and contact plan.
risks: Rare serious lung or allergic reactions

agents.name: Oxaliplatin
agents.explanation: Oxaliplatin makes links within DNA. These interfere with copying and repair, which can stop a cancer cell dividing. Healthy tissues can also be affected.
agents.watch: Cold can trigger tingling or throat discomfort. Tell the team about persistent numbness, difficulty with buttons or walking, or infusion symptoms. New breathing difficulty always needs assessment.
risks: Persistent sensory neuropathy, sometimes lasting after treatment
Rare serious lung or blood complications

agents.name: Folinic acid
agents.explanation: Folinic acid helps fluorouracil remain bound to an enzyme needed to make DNA. In this regimen it increases fluorouracil activity and can also increase its unwanted effects. It is not a vitamin supplement to start yourself.
agents.watch: The combined treatment can increase mouth soreness and diarrhoea. Report these promptly. Rare allergic reactions can occur.

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil interferes with the production and use of DNA and RNA, the instructions cells need to grow. The infusion extends exposure over approximately two days.
agents.watch: Diarrhoea, mouth sores and skin soreness may become serious. Chest pain during the pump infusion needs emergency assessment. Unexpected severe early toxicity can occur even after DPD testing.
risks: Severe early toxicity including DPD-related toxicity

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Will I need a port or a PICC?
questions.a: The team chooses the most suitable access device with you. A port is under the skin; a PICC enters through the upper arm and has an external section. Both require specific care, and the pump can be used with either.

questions.q: Does disconnecting the pump remove my port?
questions.a: No. At the arranged visit the pump is disconnected and the line cared for. A port needle may be removed, but the implanted port stays under the skin until a separate removal procedure is arranged.

questions.q: What if the pump finishes early or still looks full?
questions.a: Contact the team for advice. Do not change delivery settings or disconnect or reconnect it yourself. Follow only the specific emergency steps you have been taught.

questions.q: Is delayed diarrhoea the same as cramps during infusion?
questions.a: No. Irinotecan can cause an early reaction with cramps, sweating or diarrhoea, and a later diarrhoea problem. Tell the nurse about early symptoms and follow the separate written plan at home.

questions.q: Does the wallet QR contain my treatment record?
questions.a: No. The printed QR opens this regimen’s patient information. Your cycle stamps, appointments, test results and treatment changes remain in your own records and the clinical record.

questions.q: Can I use the printed information without a phone?
questions.a: Yes. The three-page summary, full handbook and passport can be printed. Ask your team to write the next appointments and working contact numbers on the paper copies.

phases_note: There is no fixed number of cycles for every patient. The team reviews benefit, side effects and your priorities; a break, maintenance approach or drug change needs an individual decision.
medicines_title: Your medicines and what they do
timeline_note: Bars show planned treatment and possible symptom patterns, not measured risk. Side effects can overlap and persist.
safety_note: There are no guaranteed safe days. Act on fever, sudden illness or a new serious symptom whenever it occurs. Do not wait for the next appointment.
teachback: Can you explain which medicines you are receiving, the schedule, the contact plan and the symptoms that need prompt help?
consent_support: Confirm the individual aim, likely benefit and alternatives, DPD result, the 48-hour pump, disconnection and urgent contacts. Explain early irinotecan symptoms separately from delayed diarrhoea. Explain cold sensitivity and potentially persistent neuropathy.
urgent_extra: Fever, shivers or sudden illness needs immediate oncology advice. Chest pain, collapse or severe breathing difficulty needs emergency help. Call urgently for severe or persistent diarrhoea, severe abdominal pain, inability to drink, reduced urine or a line/pump problem.

items.title: Why this treatment?
items.text: FOLFOXIRI combines three chemotherapy medicines with folinic acid to treat colorectal cancer that has spread. The aim is cancer control, symptom relief and, for selected people, a response that allows further local treatment after specialist review.

items.title: What studies can tell us
items.text: In a randomised study of people starting treatment for metastatic colorectal cancer, FOLFOXIRI improved tumour response and time before progression compared with FOLFIRI, and the study found a survival benefit. The more intensive combination also caused more severe side effects, including low white-cell counts, diarrhoea and nerve symptoms. These group results do not predict an individual outcome.

items.title: Review and your priorities
items.text: Ask when benefit will be reviewed and which symptoms, scans or tests will be used. Discuss work, caring responsibilities, time at home and what matters most to you. Delaying or reducing a medicine can be necessary for safety and does not itself prove treatment has failed.

chapters.title: Your treatment schedule
chapters.intro: Use your prescription and team-confirmed calendar.

items.title: Medicines and sequence
items.text: On Day 1, irinotecan 165 mg/m² is infused over 90 minutes, followed by oxaliplatin 85 mg/m² and folinic acid 200 mg/m² over two hours. Fluorouracil 3,200 mg/m² is then delivered continuously over 48 hours. This regimen has no fluorouracil bolus. The team confirms your prescribed doses and disconnection time.

items.title: How long treatment lasts
items.text: There is no fixed number of cycles for everyone. Treatment is reviewed against cancer control, side effects and your priorities. A change to maintenance or a break is an individual decision.

items.title: The disconnection appointment
items.text: The fluorouracil infusion lasts 48 hours from connection. Arrange the completion visit before leaving the unit. Pump removal does not remove an implanted port: the port remains until a separate procedure is arranged.

chapters.title: Before, during and after treatment
chapters.intro: Testing detects problems that may not cause symptoms.

items.title: Before the first dose
items.text: Blood count, kidney and liver tests and DPD testing are required before fluoropyrimidine treatment unless the DPD test has already been done. DPD helps the body clear fluorouracil; deficiency changes the treatment plan. A normal result does not exclude all severe toxicity.

items.title: Before each cycle
items.text: Blood count, kidney and liver results and symptoms are reviewed before each cycle. Neuropathy is assessed every cycle; report troublesome symptoms sooner. Missing results are not assumed normal.

items.title: Heart tests are conditional
items.text: Tell the team about heart disease and previous chest symptoms. An ECG is needed when cardiac function is compromised or clinical findings warrant it. There is no automatic recurring echocardiogram schedule for every patient.

items.title: Scans, markers and aftercare
items.text: Your consultant decides response scans, tumour-marker use and follow-up according to your cancer and treatment aim. This regimen does not set one scan or marker interval for everyone. Unresolved side effects or abnormal blood results need a follow-up plan.

chapters.title: Bowel symptoms and hydration
chapters.intro: Act early; do not wait for the next appointment.

items.title: Keep the written plan
items.text: Record the change from your usual bowel pattern, including stoma output. Keep the prescribed diarrhoea medicine and your oncology contact details available. Ask for specific instructions before the first treatment.

items.title: Two different irinotecan reactions
items.text: During or soon after infusion, cramps, sweating, a runny nose or diarrhoea can be an early cholinergic reaction: tell the nurse immediately. Diarrhoea starting more than 24 hours later needs the separate prescribed delayed-diarrhoea plan, which may differ from packet instructions. If it persists despite that plan, or you become unwell, seek urgent advice.

items.title: Urgent symptoms
items.text: Contact oncology urgently for persistent diarrhoea, inability to drink, reduced urine, dizziness, blood in stools, fever or severe abdominal pain. Do not assume severe abdominal pain is an ordinary treatment effect. A stoma can make fluid loss less obvious: report a marked increase in output.

chapters.title: Cold sensitivity and longer-lasting nerve symptoms
chapters.intro: These are two related but different oxaliplatin problems.

items.title: Cold-triggered symptoms
items.text: Cold drinks, cold air and cold objects can bring on tingling or throat sensations. Avoid triggers and do not use ice chips during oxaliplatin treatment. New breathing difficulty still needs urgent assessment; it must not be diagnosed at home as simply a cold reaction.

items.title: Persistent neuropathy
items.text: Report numbness, tingling, pain or difficulty doing buttons, writing, holding objects or walking. Symptoms can accumulate over cycles and sometimes persist after treatment. Explain how long symptoms lasted and what activities changed.

items.title: Review before more oxaliplatin
items.text: Nerve assessment is required each cycle for this regimen. The team may change or stop oxaliplatin independently of the other medicines to reduce the risk of lasting harm. Do not wait for a scheduled assessment if symptoms are worsening.

items.title: Mouth and hands or feet
items.text: Fluorouracil can cause mouth ulcers and painful redness or peeling of hands and feet. Report symptoms early, especially if eating, drinking, walking or using your hands becomes difficult. Ask for non-irritating mouth care and skin-care advice.

items.title: Nausea, appetite and fatigue
items.text: Use the anti-sickness prescription and call if it is not controlling symptoms. Small regular meals and manageable activity with rest may help daily routines. Fatigue can have several causes; persistent or worsening fatigue may need blood tests or review. Irinotecan may also cause hair thinning or loss; ask about practical support.

items.title: Low blood counts and infection
items.text: Chemotherapy can reduce white cells, red cells and platelets. Fever, shivers or sudden illness needs immediate oncology advice, even if your temperature is not raised. Follow the unit’s temperature instructions and do not wait for a scheduled blood test. Unusual bruising, bleeding, breathlessness or marked weakness also needs review.

items.title: Heart and infusion symptoms
items.text: Fluorouracil can rarely cause serious heart problems. Chest pain, collapse or severe breathing difficulty needs emergency assessment. Tell the nurse immediately if flushing, swelling, wheeze, rash or pain occurs during an infusion.

chapters.title: Your line and home pump
chapters.intro: Ask for a demonstration and show the team what you would do.

items.title: Access and ordinary care
items.text: The team selects a port, PICC or other suitable access with you. Keep dressings and connections secure and follow the specific washing, bathing and activity instructions. Keep the pump away from excessive heat or cold.

items.title: Leak, disconnection or unexpected flow
items.text: Call the oncology contact for a leaking or disconnected pump, pain/swelling at the line, a pump that finishes early, or one that appears not to be delivering. Do not change settings or reconnect or disconnect the device unless specifically trained and instructed. Follow the spill/emergency steps the unit has taught you.

items.title: Disconnection and future care
items.text: The pump is disconnected at the arranged visit and the line is cared for. A port needle can be removed while the implanted port stays under the skin. Ask when any dressing changes, flushes or later line removal are due.

chapters.title: Supportive medicines and daily life
chapters.intro: The prescription changes with the active treatment.

items.title: Your supportive prescription
items.text: Confirm prevention and rescue medicines for nausea, the diarrhoea plan and any growth-factor injections. Atropine may be used before irinotecan for the early reaction; mention glaucoma and asthma. Do not duplicate anti-sickness medicines, start supplements or take leftover prescriptions without checking with the oncology pharmacist.

items.title: Medicines and interactions
items.text: Bring all prescribed and non-prescribed medicines, supplements and anticoagulants to review. Tell the team before starting antibiotics or a new medicine. Do not independently stop regular treatment such as anticoagulants before a procedure.

items.title: Fertility, pregnancy and sex
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before starting where relevant. Ask which contraception, pregnancy, breastfeeding and sex precautions apply during treatment and after the last dose. The period depends on your medicines and circumstances.

items.title: Practical support
items.text: Ask about work, driving, travel, nutrition, caring responsibilities and emotional support. Report symptoms in terms of what you can eat, drink or do. An interpreter, another explanation or a written plan can help you and a chosen family member or carer.

chapters.title: Your paper plan, wallet card and contacts
chapters.intro: The three-page summary and handbook are usable without a phone.

items.title: Carry the treatment card
items.text: The example telephone numbers on the wallet card are placeholders. Your team must replace them with working daytime and out-of-hours numbers before patient use. Keep the card with you; the QR opens the regimen information, not your confidential medical record.

items.title: Cycle and phase record
items.text: Ask the team to stamp or write the treatment actually given. For an open-ended course, use the passport for additional cycle records; blank spaces are not a prescribed number of treatments.

items.title: Before leaving
items.text: Confirm your next tests and appointments, pump disconnection when relevant, medicines to take at home and how to obtain urgent help. Explain the plan back in your own words; ask for anything unclear to be written down.

day_groups.title: Infusion and pump connection
day_groups.body: The team checks symptoms, blood results and the active treatment plan. Day-ward infusions are followed by connection of the fluorouracil pump.
day_groups.action: Before leaving, confirm the pump-care instructions, disconnection appointment and contact number.

day_groups.title: The pump is delivering treatment
day_groups.body: The pump runs for approximately 48 hours from connection. Keep the device and line secure and dry as taught. The team confirms the actual disconnection appointment.
day_groups.action: Call for a leaking, disconnected or unexpectedly stopped pump. Do not reconnect, alter settings or disconnect it yourself unless specifically trained and instructed.

day_groups.title: After disconnection
day_groups.body: Delayed diarrhoea can begin after the first 24 hours and may continue after pump removal. Use your written plan and contact the team early. Cold-triggered tingling may occur and nerve symptoms can persist. Nausea and tiredness can overlap; symptoms are not restricted to these days.
day_groups.action: Report poor intake, persistent diarrhoea or mouth pain early. Chest pain or major breathing difficulty requires emergency help.

day_groups.title: Between visits and the next review
day_groups.body: Blood counts can fall between visits. Tell the team about bowel symptoms, mouth pain and how you are managing daily activities. Treatment proceeds only after review.
day_groups.action: Bring the symptom passport and check the next appointment. Day 1 usually repeats 14 days after this cycle started, only if confirmed.

support.title: Nausea prevention and rescue
support.text: This chemotherapy combination has a high risk of sickness without prevention. Follow the prescribed prevention and rescue medicines. Call if vomiting prevents drinking; do not duplicate steroids or anti-sickness doses.

support.title: Blood counts and recovery
support.text: Growth-factor injections depend on your risk, blood counts and previous complications. If prescribed, confirm their timing in relation to chemotherapy and pump removal; do not assume everyone receives them.

support.title: Early and delayed diarrhoea plans
support.text: Atropine is normally prescribed before irinotecan for early cramps, sweating or diarrhoea. It is avoided with glaucoma; tell the team about asthma as well. At home use the separately prescribed delayed-diarrhoea instructions. This can differ from standard over-the-counter dosing. Keep the medicine and urgent-contact plan available.

support.title: Cold and mouth care
support.text: Avoid cold drinks, cold air and cold objects if they trigger symptoms. Do not use ice chips during oxaliplatin treatment. Ask for non-cold mouth-care advice. New breathing difficulty must still be assessed rather than assumed to be a cold reaction.

evidence.title: Understanding the evidence
evidence.intro: Ask which study population and treatment sequence match your plan.
evidence.population: Previously untreated metastatic colorectal cancer; FOLFOXIRI compared with FOLFIRI.
evidence.interpretation: In a randomised study of people starting treatment for metastatic colorectal cancer, FOLFOXIRI improved tumour response and time before progression compared with FOLFIRI, and the study found a survival benefit. The more intensive combination also caused more severe side effects, including low white-cell counts, diarrhoea and nerve symptoms. These group results do not predict an individual outcome.

chronology_notes.title: Day ward and home pump
chronology_notes.text: Day 1 infusions lead into a 48-hour pump. The disconnection visit is arranged from the actual connection time.

chronology_notes.title: Two different bowel reactions
chronology_notes.text: Cramps and sweating during infusion need immediate nursing attention. Diarrhoea starting more than 24 hours later needs the separate written home plan and early contact.

chronology_notes.title: No safe window
chronology_notes.text: Fever, sudden illness or a serious symptom needs action on any day, including after pump removal.

chronology_notes.title: Between visits
chronology_notes.text: Record symptoms and their effects on drinking, eating, bowel/stoma output, mobility and usual activities.

chronology_notes.title: Treatment review
chronology_notes.text: There is no fixed number of cycles for every patient. The team reviews benefit, side effects and your priorities; a break, maintenance approach or drug change needs an individual decision.

monitoring_schedule.note: Required checks are shown explicitly. ECG, additional urine tests and anticoagulant tests apply only when indicated. Scans and tumour markers follow your individual cancer plan; this page does not prescribe a universal surveillance interval. Confirm who books and reviews each test.

sections.title: Before starting
sections.text: Confirm the aim, DPD result, test appointments, prescribed supportive medicines and working urgent contact numbers. Bring your full medicines list, including supplements.

sections.title: Line, pump and disconnection
sections.text: Agree the access device and care training. The pump runs for 48 hours; confirm the disconnection appointment from its connection time. Do not alter settings, disconnect or reconnect it unless specifically trained and instructed.

sections.title: If the plan changes
sections.text: The team confirms the next treatment, blood-test and supportive-medicine dates after a delay or dose change. Do not use a previous calendar as a prescription.

sections.title: Contacts, paper copies and QR
sections.text: The example telephone numbers on the wallet card are placeholders. Your team must replace them with working daytime and out-of-hours numbers before patient use. Keep the card with you; the QR opens the regimen information, not your confidential medical record.
